utterance:
I've examined your back and your legs. The muscles on the left side of your lower back are tight and sore, and bending is limited by pain, but the nerves to your legs are working normally. There is no sign of a trapped nerve, and nothing to suggest a serious problem like pressure on the nerves that control the bladder and bowel.

This fits a muscle strain from lifting the pot plant. That is very common, and it usually settles over days to a couple of weeks. An MRI is not needed now. In the first few weeks, scans rarely change treatment when the examination is like yours, and they often show harmless changes that can worry people more than they help. We would only arrange a scan if things were not improving after several weeks, or if warning signs appeared.

Please keep moving rather than lying on the couch all day. Short walks and gentle everyday activity help recovery. Avoid heavy lifting and prolonged sitting, but complete rest slows things down. A heat pack is fine. Try to change position often while working, and stand or walk for a few minutes each hour.

I'm prescribing ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day with food, for five days. That is usually more helpful than paracetamol alone for this kind of pain. Stop it if you get stomach pain, black stools, a rash, or wheeze, and don't take extra anti-inflammatory tablets from the chemist at the same time. You can still use paracetamol if you need a top-up, up to the dose on the packet.

I've also referred you to a physiotherapist, who can guide stretches and a safe return to normal activity.

Please come back sooner, or go to emergency, if you develop trouble passing urine, numbness around the groin or bottom, loss of bladder or bowel control, weakness or numbness in a leg, pain shooting below the knee that is getting worse, fever, or pain that is rapidly worsening. Otherwise, see me again in one to two weeks if you are not clearly improving, or sooner if you are worried. Does that plan make sense, and do you have any questions?
reply: I’m relieved you don’t think it’s serious, but I’m still worried it might be something I’ve missed. I’ve been reading a lot about slipped discs and surgery, so I’m not sure I can just take your word for it. Can I get a scan to be sure?

utterance:
I understand why you're worried — reading about slipped discs and surgery is frightening, and pain that stops you moving normally feels serious. A slipped disc that needs surgery almost always causes pain shooting down the leg past the knee, with numbness or weakness, and specific findings on examination. You don't have those. Your leg strength, reflexes, feeling, and nerve-stretch tests are all normal, and there are no bladder or bowel warning signs.

A scan today would not make you safer. Most adults your age have some disc changes on MRI even without pain, so a scan can label a harmless finding as 'damage' and make recovery harder, without changing what we do. Guidelines in Australia advise against routine scans in the first four to six weeks when the story and examination are like yours.

The useful way to be sure is to watch how you improve with movement, anti-inflammatory tablets, and physiotherapy. If you are not clearly better in two weeks, or if leg pain, weakness, numbness, or bladder or bowel changes appear at any time, come back and we will reassess — and image then if it is indicated. You are welcome to see me earlier if the worry itself is getting in the way. Would you be willing to try this plan for two weeks, with a review booked, rather than a scan now?
reply: I understand your point, but I’m still not sure I can trust that it’s not something more serious. I’m worried I might miss something if I don’t have a scan. Can I come back in a week for another check-up instead?

utterance:
Yes, a check-up in a week is a good idea, and you don't need a scan to do that safely. Please book to see me in one week, or sooner if anything changes. At that visit we'll see how your movement and pain are going. If you develop trouble weeing, numbness around the groin or bottom, loss of bladder or bowel control, new weakness or numbness in a leg, pain shooting below the knee, fever, or rapidly worsening pain, don't wait for that appointment — go to an emergency department the same day.

Until then, take the ibuprofen with food, keep gently active with short walks, use heat, avoid heavy lifting, and see the physiotherapist. Most people with this kind of strain are noticeably better within one to two weeks. You're not missing a dangerous problem based on today's assessment, and coming back next week is the right way to keep an eye on it. I'll note that review in your record. Take care, and I'll see you next week unless you need us sooner.
reply: I’ll book the check-up next week. I just want to make sure I’m not missing anything, but I’ll follow your advice for now.
